passage:
My brother Ojas has a friend, Kashish, who calls him whenever things go wrong. Last Sunday Kashish came over, eyes swollen, and asked to stay with us 'for a few months' after a fight with his landlord.
I expected Ojas to say yes. He always does. Instead he sat close, listened for a whole hour, and said, 'That sounds awful. Being told to leave with a week's notice, I'd be scared too.'
Then, gently: 'You can stay this weekend. Not months. On Monday I'll help you look at rooms near your office.'
Kashish looked hurt for a second. Then he nodded.
I don't know what Ojas felt. His hands were clasped tight. But on Monday the two of them were on the laptop, shortlisting rooms, and Kashish was laughing.

qa.q: How long did Ojas say Kashish could stay?
qa.a: This weekend, not months.

qa.q: What might Ojas's tightly clasped hands suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: They might suggest saying no was hard for him, torn between caring for Kashish and holding his limit.

qa.q: What choice did Ojas make that combined empathy with a boundary?
qa.a: He listened for an hour and named Kashish's fear, then offered only the weekend plus help looking at rooms on Monday.

qa.q: How might Kashish see Ojas after Monday?
qa.a: Kashish may feel both supported and respected, getting real help to stand on his own rather than just a place to hide.

grounding: Shows, through a sibling's eyes, a young adult who understands a friend's fear without agreeing to everything, keeping a firm but kind boundary.

passage:
Monday: Himani came to Lavanya's desk in tears. 'The report's due tomorrow and I can't. Could you just do the charts?' Lavanya had done the charts last month too, and she felt the old pull to say yes.
She said instead, 'I can see you're really stressed. I won't do them, but I'll sit with you for twenty minutes and we'll plan it.' Himani's face fell.
Tuesday: Himani stayed late, grumbling, and finished the charts herself. Two were wrong. She fixed them.
Two weeks later: Himani stopped by with chai. 'I was annoyed with you,' she admitted. 'But I actually know how to do charts now.' Lavanya laughed. 'And I actually got my own work done.'

qa.q: What did Himani ask Lavanya to do?
qa.a: Just do the charts for the report.

qa.q: What did Lavanya feel when Himani asked again?
qa.a: Lavanya felt torn, tempted by the old pull to say yes and rescue Himani, having done the charts last month too.

qa.q: What choice did Lavanya make on Monday, and how did it help both of them?
qa.a: She named Himani's stress but offered twenty minutes of planning instead of doing the charts; Himani learned the skill and Lavanya finished her own work.

qa.q: How did Himani's view of Lavanya's refusal change over two weeks?
qa.a: At first Himani was annoyed, but later came to value it because she now knows how to do charts.

grounding: Shows a young adult who understands Himani's stress without rescuing her, and how empathy alongside a firm boundary helps both over time.

passage: Parveen, you asked how to say no to someone you love. When I was twenty-four, my younger brother Arif kept asking me for money. First for a phone, then a trip, then to pay back a friend. Each time he cried, and I felt every tear as if it were mine. I gave, and gave. One night he asked again, and I, Nazia, did something new. I held his hand and said, "I can see how scared you are. I'm not giving you money this time. But I'll sit with you while you call Abbu and tell him the truth." He shouted at me. Then he called. It was the best thing I ever did for him. Understanding someone, beta, doesn't mean doing everything they ask.

qa.q: What was the third thing Arif wanted money for?
qa.a: To pay back a friend.

qa.q: How did young Nazia feel each time Arif cried?
qa.a: Nazia felt every tear as if it were Nazia's own, pulled to give because of Arif's distress.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Nazia named Arif's fear but refused the money, offering to sit with him while he called Abbu.

qa.q: How did Arif react to the refusal?
qa.a: He shouted at first, then called Abbu and told the truth.

grounding: Shows an adult who understands a sibling's fear yet refuses to rescue, pairing empathy with a firm boundary.

passage: It was ten at night, the quarterly report was due at nine the next morning, and Noor was on Manjula's doorstep, crying. "Please, can you finish my section too? My mother's been shouting all week, I can't think." Manjula felt the pull at once; she could see how frazzled Noor was, how her hands shook. The old Manjula would have said yes and worked till dawn. She made tea instead. "That sounds really hard, Noor. I'm so sorry about home." She listened for twenty minutes. Then: "I can't write your section. I'll sit with you for an hour while you start it, and I'll help you ask the manager for a day's extension." Noor looked stung. Then she nodded and opened her laptop.

qa.q: When was the quarterly report due?
qa.a: At nine the next morning.

qa.q: What did Manjula feel when she saw Noor crying?
qa.a: She felt a strong pull of sympathy and the old urge to rescue by saying yes.

qa.q: How did Manjula combine empathy with a boundary?
qa.a: She listened and acknowledged Noor's pain, refused to write the section, and offered an hour of company and help asking for an extension.

qa.q: How did Noor react to the boundary?
qa.a: Noor looked stung, then nodded and started working.

grounding: Illustrates an adult who understands a friend's distress without giving in, holding a firm, kind boundary under time pressure.

passage: Rekha's younger brother Hrithik turned up at her Bandra flat with red eyes and a request. He had failed two papers and wanted her to tell their parents he was staying with her "to study", so he could skip going home for Diwali. "You get it, Didi. Papa will explode." She did get it. She remembered her own first failed exam, the dread of the phone call. "I understand why you're scared," she said, sitting beside him. "And I'm not going to lie to them for you." His face fell. "But I'll come with you on Friday and be in the room when you tell them. And afterwards we'll make a study plan together." Hrithik stared at the floor. Then he said, very quietly, "Okay."

qa.q: How many papers had Hrithik failed?
qa.a: Two papers.

qa.q: How was Hrithik feeling when he came to Rekha?
qa.a: He was scared and upset, red-eyed and dreading his father's reaction.

qa.q: What makes Rekha's response both empathetic and firm?
qa.a: She named his fear and remembered her own, but refused to lie and offered to be there when he told them.

qa.q: How might their parents react on Friday, with Rekha in the room?
qa.a: They may still be upset, but calmer, seeing the two of them face it honestly together.

grounding: Shows a young adult understanding a sibling's fear without agreeing to lie, pairing empathy with a firm boundary.

passage:
"Harsha, please. Just draft the client report tonight. I'm drowning," Farida said, leaning on his desk.
"You really are. You've had the audit, the new hire and your mum's surgery, all in one month."
"So you'll do it?"
"No. I can't write your report again."
Her face fell. "Wow. I thought you were on my side."
"I am. That's why I'm saying no. Last time you felt worse when the manager asked you questions about it."
Farida sat down heavily. "That was awful."
"Here's what I can do. I'll sit with you from six to seven and we'll outline it together. And tomorrow you could ask the manager for two extra days."
She was quiet, then gave a small, tired laugh. "You're annoying when you're right."
"I know. Get your laptop."

qa.q: What did Farida ask Harsha to do tonight?
qa.a: She asked him to draft the client report tonight.

qa.q: How did Farida feel when Harsha said no?
qa.a: She felt hurt and let down at first, saying she thought he was on her side, then tired and reluctantly relieved.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who wants to support a stressed friend without rescuing them?
qa.a: Name what they are going through, refuse the thing that would harm them, and offer a clear, limited kind of help like Harsha's hour together.

qa.q: What would change if Harsha had simply written the report?
qa.a: Farida would feel rescued tonight but might face another awful meeting and depend on him again, and Harsha could start to feel used.

grounding: Harsha understands Farida's stress without writing her report for her, showing empathy beside a firm boundary.
